title: Los Angeles clipping: Picou sits in with Dizzy Gillespie
summary: An article on Picou's visit to Los Angeles, his view of bebop and Dizzy Gillespie, his compositions and his dance tunes.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: the Municipal Auditorium, Celestan and Piku slated for awards. See if there's anything in here to read. This must have been an interview in Los Angeles, though. I'll read a little of this. The unharmonized staccato-like rhythm that is bebop might not be here to stay, says Alphonse Piku, but it certainly will take its place in the annals of American jazz history. One of the nation's foremost clarinetists and originators of Dixieland jazz, Piku, a native of New Orleans, took time out last week to sit in with the international famous bebop king, Dizzy Gillespie. Did you play with him out there one night? I was, sure. You did? At frequent intervals, Piku said Americans undergo a decided change in their modern music, which is added to, more or less, a slight deviation from another style designed to satisfy chiefly the dancing fancies of the younger generation. Let's see what's next. Well then, thus at the change of the century, ragtime was the music rave of the day. Then came Dixieland, jazz, swing, and now bebop. Giving rise to these music styles were such dances as Walking the Dog, Cakewalk, Charleston, Lindy Hop, Jersey Bounce, and Modern Box.
What was that Walking the Dog?

Remember that tune? I have the sheet music for that. I think I was by Shelton Brooks. Yeah, Walking the Dog, yeah. He's the one who wrote Darktown Strutters Ball. They played that down here then too, did they? I think that came from Chicago. It says, Piku, whose music aggregation was Tops at the turn of the century, has been actively engaged in music for almost 50 years. That's right. And Dixieland jazz was his first love and he continues to play it in his native city of New Orleans where he heads a seven-piece orchestra. That's right. Composer of such well-known tunes as High Society. That's right. Onzaga Blues. Yeah. Olympia Rag. Yeah, Olympia Rag. And Snake Blues. Yeah, Snake Blues. I think that's when King Oliver recorded it. I believe he called it Snake Rag. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I remember your name is on that record. Yeah, that's right. And the diminutive, I can't pronounce it, Creole readily recalls playing with such musical greats as Louis Armstrong, King Oliver, Manuel Perez, and others. That's right. Then it talks a little bit about Dizzy Gillespie again. Oh, here, in Los Angeles, to visit with his daughter, Mrs. Olga Piku. It should be Miss Olga, isn't it? And here's a misprint or something. It's a three-month stay. Oh, that's a married name. Yeah. You were there for three months then. So that's the end of that article. Let's see what's on the next page. Well, here's a picture of you with the brass band cap on. Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. That's me right there. This looks like it might have been out of Ebony or something. That's my clarinet, what I got right now. Yes, yes. Right now. You see this little bell on the end there? Yes. I got it. It says under the caption, Dixieland musicians still playing in New Orleans are Alphonse Piku, 70, famous original Creole band clarinetist and Oscar Papacelostan, 64. That's why.
